content: Knock knees, also known as genu valgum, is a condition where the knees touch each other while the ankles remain apart when standing. This results in the legs angling inward. In infants, bowlegs are common due to their folded position in the uterus. As the child begins to walk, typically between 12 to 18 months of age, the bowlegs start to straighten. By the age of 3, many children naturally develop knock knees, where the knees touch but the ankles remain separated when standing. By puberty, the legs usually straighten out, allowing most children to stand with both their knees and ankles touching without forcing the position. Knock knees can also arise due to underlying medical conditions or diseases. These include: Injury to the shinbone, which may result in knock knees on only one leg. Osteomyelitis, a bone infection. Obesity or being overweight. Rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency. If a healthcare provider suspects that knock knees are due to a cause other than normal development, they will conduct a thorough examination and review the child’s medical history. Additional diagnostic studies may be ordered to identify the underlying cause. Parents should seek medical evaluation if they suspect their child has knock knees. While knock knees are typically not treated, intervention may be necessary if the condition persists beyond the age of 7. In such cases, a night brace attached to a shoe or orthopedic shoe may be recommended. Surgery might be considered for severe cases that persist into late childhood, especially if the separation between the ankles is significant. Children generally outgrow knock knees without treatment unless the condition is caused by an underlying disease. For cases requiring surgical intervention, the procedure typically yields good cosmetic outcomes. Possible complications of untreated knock knees include: Difficulty walking, though this is very rare. Changes in self-esteem due to the cosmetic appearance of the condition. Early onset of knee arthritis if the condition is left unaddressed. There is no known method to prevent the development of normal knock knees.
